papers.title_in_file: Quantum annealing with more than one hundred qubits (arXiv:1304.4595v2, 21 Jul 2013; main text pp.1-6 and Supplementary material pp.7-23)
papers.version_note: The file is the arXiv v2 preprint of Boixo et al., titled 'Quantum annealing with more than one hundred qubits'. The record name says 'Evidence for quantum annealing with more than one hundred qubits'; the file name (2013-04) matches that earlier title. The content is the paper the record names. The Supplementary material numbers its own pages 1 to 17 and its figures from 1 to 33 again, so this entry labels them 'Supplementary Figure N'.
sections_read: Supplementary II. The chimera graph of the D-Wave device
Supplementary III. Classical algorithms (A. Simulated annealing, B. Simulated quantum annealing, C. Exact solvers)

Supplementary IV. Success probability histograms (A. Experimental annealing histograms, B. Simulated annealing and simulated quantum annealing, C. Hardness, gaps and free qubits, D. Improving the final state by fixing single spin errors)
Supplementary V. Correlations (A. Copulae, B. Reproducibility, C. Gauge averaging, D. Correlations for the simulated annealer)
Supplementary VI. Scaling (A. Scaling of the exact solvers, B. Optimising the total annealing time, C. Detecting quantum speed up)

figures.shows: Four histograms of success probability (x, 0 to 1) against probability distribution (y, 0 to about 0.25; 0 to about 0.5 in panel D) for N = 108 qubits and 1000 spin glass instances. A) D-Wave device, gauge averaged: bimodal, small peak near 0 and larger peak near 1. B) simulated quantum annealing: bimodal, with a tall peak near 1 of about 0.2. C) simulated classical annealing: unimodal broad hump around the middle, peak near about 0.4 to 0.5. D) spin dynamics: a very tall bar near 0 of about 0.45 and a smaller bar near 1.
figures.confirmed_by: In contrast, the D-Wave device, the simulated quantum annealer and the spin dynamics model exhibit a bimodal distribution, with a clear split into easy and hard instances.

figures.shows: Four heat maps of the joint probability distribution p(s, Delta) (colour scale, log from 10^-6 to 10^0). x: success probability s (0 to 1); y: energy difference Delta above the ground state (0 to 20). Panels: A) DW, B) SQA, C) SA, D) SD. DW and SQA look alike (weight at low Delta for high s, higher Delta for low s); SA is concentrated at intermediate s; SD shows weight at higher Delta.
figures.confirmed_by: We ﬁnd very similar results for the D-Wave device (panel A) and the simulated quantum annealer (panel B).

figures.shows: Density scatter plots (colour scale of instances per pixel, 0 to 20) of success probabilities, axes 0 to 1. A) DW gauge mean set II against set I (baseline). B) DW gauge averaged against SQA. C) DW gauge averaged against SD. D) mean Hamming distance of excited states (y, 0 to about 70) against success probability (x), N = 108 with local fields. Panels A and B concentrate along the diagonal and in the lower left and upper right corners; C shows little diagonal structure; D shows small Hamming distance at high success probability.
figures.confirmed_by: Panel B) shows a scatter plot of the hardness of instances for the simulated quantum annealer and the D-Wave device after gauge averaging.

figures.shows: Two panels of the gap between ground state and lowest excited state in units of temperature (Delta/T, y) against Gamma = A(t)/B(t) (x, 0 to 3), blue points with a red horizontal line at Delta/T of about 1. Left (easy instance): the gap rises to about 3 near Gamma of about 1.5, falls near Gamma of about 2.3. Right (hard instance): the gap stays lower, peaking at about 1.5, with additional low points near Gamma of about 0.5.
figures.confirmed_by: In the left panel we show the gap for an “easy” instance with success probability 98% and on the right for a “hard” instance with success probability 8%.

figures.shows: Three log-scale panels against linear problem size sqrt(N) from 8 to 512. A) DW gauge averaged: total time (y, about 10^-7 to 10^0 s) with percentile curves 1% to 99%; the median rises from about 5 microseconds slowly; the 99% curve rises steeply to about 10^-2 s. B) SA: total effort in spin flips (y, about 10^4 to 10^11) with arrows marking 1 ms on GPU, CPU 8 cores and CPU 1 core. C) SQA: total effort in spin updates times beta, with arrows for 1 s on CPU 8 cores and 1 core. All curves in B and C rise roughly exponentially in sqrt(N).
figures.confirmed_by: Shown is the scaling of the total eﬀort to ﬁnd the ground state with 99% probability for A) the D-Wave device, B) the simulated annealer and C) the simulated quantum annealer.

figures.shows: The chimera graph of the D-Wave One Rainer chip: 4 by 4 unit cells of eight qubits, qubits numbered 0 to 127; working qubits in green, non-working in grey, couplers as black lines.
figures.confirmed_by: The D-Wave One Rainer chip consists of 4 × 4 unit cells of eight qubits

figures.shows: A) density scatter of success probabilities, discrete-time against continuous-time quantum Monte Carlo (0 to 1 each axis), scattered around the diagonal. B) two independent continuous-time Monte Carlo runs with different seeds: points lie very close to the diagonal. Colour scale of instances 0 to 20.
figures.confirmed_by: Correlation between simulated quantum annealers. Axes corresponds to success probabilities and pixels are colour-coded according to the number of instances.

figures.shows: Annealing schedules A(t) and B(t) against time t (0 to 1). A) Schedule I, linear: A falls from 1.0 to 0 and B rises from 0 to about 1.0 (units a.u., axis 0 to 2). B) Schedule II, the D-Wave schedule (energy in GHz, 0 to about 5): A starts near 5, falls quickly then slowly to 0 near t about 0.6; B rises from near 0, accelerating, to about 5 at t = 1.
figures.confirmed_by: Annealing schedules used for Monte Carlo codes A) schedule I, the linear schedule. B) schedule II, the schedule of the D-Wave device.

figures.shows: Success probability histograms (x 0 to 1, y 0 to 0.5) for the D-Wave device without local fields at A) 58, B) 84, C) 87 and D) 108 qubits. A tall peak near 1 in each; the peak near 0 grows from small in A to about 0.1 in C and D.
figures.confirmed_by: The peak at low success probability grows with the number of qubits, reﬂecting the increasing hardness of the corresponding problem instances.

figures.shows: Success probability histograms (x 0 to 1, y 0 to 0.5) for the D-Wave device with local fields at A) 58, B) 85, C) 87 and D) 108 qubits. Tall peak near 1 in each (about 0.3 to 0.45); small peak near 0.
figures.confirmed_by: Success probability histograms for the D-Wave device for instances with local ﬁelds. A) using 58 qubits, B) 85 qubits, C) 87 qubits and D) 108 qubits.

figures.shows: Overlaid histograms of success probability for instances with no field (blue) and with field (red). A) simulated classical annealer with 50 sweeps: unimodal, peaks at low success probability (about 0.1 to 0.3), field case shifted slightly to higher success. B) simulated quantum annealer with 10,000 sweeps: bimodal; the peak near 1 is larger for the with-field case.
figures.confirmed_by: Comparison of instances with and without local ﬁelds. A) success probability histograms for the simulated classical annealer with 50 sweeps (updates per spin).

figures.shows: Success probability histograms (x 0 to 1, y 0 to 0.4) of the simulated classical annealer for 100, 1000, 10000 and 100000 sweeps without local fields. Unimodal throughout; the peak moves from near success probability about 0.1 (100 sweeps) to about 0.3 to 0.4 (1000), broad (10000), and to a tall peak near 1 at about 0.3 (100000).
figures.confirmed_by: While in the simulated classical annealer the distribution is always unimodal and shifts towards larger success probabilities upon increasing the annealing time

figures.shows: Success probability histograms (x 0 to 1, y 0 to 0.25) of simulated quantum annealing for 3000, 5000 and 7000 sweeps, without local fields, schedule II, T = 0.1. The bimodal shape sharpens with sweeps: the peak near 1 reaches about 0.22 at 5000 and 7000 sweeps and the low peak is small.
figures.confirmed_by: The bimodal structure becomes more pronounced upon increasing the annealing time from A) 3, 000 sweeps to B) 5, 000 and C) 7, 000 sweeps.

figures.shows: Success probability histograms (x 0 to 1, y 0 to 0.25) of simulated quantum annealing at T = 0.2, 0.3, 0.5, 1.0 (7000 sweeps, no fields). At the lowest temperature a strong peak near 1 (about 0.25) and near 0 (about 0.1); at T = 1.0 the distribution is flat and low (below about 0.06).
figures.confirmed_by: The bimodal structure becomes more pronounced at lower temperature and vanishes when increasing the temperature.

figures.shows: Success histograms (x 0 to 1, y 0 to about 0.6) of simulated quantum annealing, no local fields, with 200, 288, 392 and 512 qubits. The peak near 0 grows from about 0.18 at 200 qubits to about 0.65 at 512 qubits, and the peak near 1 shrinks to nearly nothing.
figures.confirmed_by: The fraction of easy problems rapidly decreases when increasing the problem size beyond 200 spins.

figures.shows: Success histograms (x 0 to 1, y 0 to 0.5) of simulated quantum annealing with local fields at 200, 288, 392 and 512 qubits. The peak near 1 decreases from about 0.47 (200 qubits) to about 0.17 (512 qubits) while the peak near 0 grows from about 0.23 to about 0.47; both peaks persist at 512.
figures.confirmed_by: Histograms of the hardness distribution obtained by simulated quantum annealing with Nupdates = 10000 Monte Carlo updates per spin using schedule II with T = 0.1.

figures.shows: Success histograms (x 0 to 1, y 0 to 1.0) of the simulated classical annealer with 10000 updates per spin, no fields, at 128, 200, 288, 392, 512 qubits. Unimodal; the peak shifts from broad around 0.3 at 128 qubits to a tall bar near 0 of about 0.95 at 512 qubits.
figures.confirmed_by: It is seen that, in contrast to simulated quantum annealing where the weight in the two peaks of the bimodal distribution changes, here at ﬁxed annealing time the unimodal peak gradually shifts to smaller success probabilities.

figures.shows: Histogram of (free qubits in excited states minus free qubits in ground states), x from -2 to 10, y probability 0 to 0.45, for easy (blue) and hard (red) instances. Easy instances peak at about 0 to 1 (up to about 0.37); hard instances are spread over about 2 to 9 with peak near 4.
figures.confirmed_by: As seen in ﬁgure 13, hard instances tend to have more free qubits in low energy excited states.

figures.shows: A) success probability histogram for N = 108 with local fields, d = 0 (blue) against d <= 1 (red): the red bar near 1 is about 0.41 against about 0.27 blue; bars near 0 about 0.09 equal. B to E) success probability against problem size N (20 to 100) for the 90th, 50th, 5th and 1st percentile, empty symbols without and filled with single-flip correction; the 90th percentile falls from about 1 to about 0.1; the 1st percentile stays near 1.000 with correction.
figures.confirmed_by: Eﬀect of ﬁxing single spin ﬂip errors. Shown are results for N = 108 spin instances with local ﬁelds: A) Histogram of the success probability s with (d ≤ 1) and without (d = 0) single spin ﬂips.

figures.shows: Correlation (A, C) and copula (B, D) density plots of success probabilities, SQA (x) against DW (y) for A, B (single gauge) and against DW gauge averaged for C, D; red diagonal line; colour scale of instances 0 to 20. Copula panels show a band along the diagonal, strongest in the corners.
figures.confirmed_by: Correlations and copulae between the simulated quantum annealer and the D-Wave device.

figures.shows: Copula density plots of hardness for akmaxsat (x) against A) the D-Wave device, B) the simulated annealer, C) the simulated quantum annealer; diffuse speckle with no diagonal band.
figures.confirmed_by: In ﬁgure 16 we show the copulae between the hardness for akmaxsat and the D-Wave device and the simulated classical and quantum annealers. We do not observe any correlations.

figures.shows: Correlation (A, C) and copula (B, D) density plots for repeated D-Wave runs: A, B same day; C, D one month apart (y) against DW (x). Concentrated along the diagonal with a few outliers.
figures.confirmed_by: The correlations (see ﬁgure 17) show that the device is stable over the time of a month.

figures.shows: Density scatter plots of success probabilities for 1000 instances of N = 108: A) DW against SQA; B) DW against DW gauge-transformed; C) DW gauge averaged against SQA; D) DW gauge averaged against a single DW gauge. Dense in lower-left and upper-right corners; C and D show fewer extreme outliers than A and B.
figures.confirmed_by: Shown are scatter plots of correlations of the success probabilities of 1000 instances of N = 108 spins.

figures.shows: A, B) correlation and copula between two single gauge choices (DW gauge I against gauge II): wide scatter. C, D) mean of 8 gauges (set I) against mean of 8 other gauges (set II): tight diagonal band.
figures.confirmed_by: Gauge averaging signiﬁcantly increases correlations.

figures.shows: Success probability histograms (x 0 to 1, y 0 to 0.2) of 108 qubit D-Wave results averaged over 2, 8, 40 and 100 gauges. All bimodal; the low-success peak is about 0.07 and the high peak about 0.1 to 0.12; panels for 40 and 100 gauges look the same.
figures.confirmed_by: One sees that the marginal distribution converges after roughly 40 gauges.

figures.shows: Total time on the D-Wave device without gauge averaging (y, microseconds, 10^-1 to 10^6) against sqrt(N) (8 to 512) for percentile curves 1% to 99%. Low percentiles stay near about 5 microseconds; high percentiles rise steeply (99% to about 10^4 microseconds by N near 72 to 108) and are missing at larger sizes.
figures.confirmed_by: The higher percentiles are not shown for large systems since 1000 repetitions of the annealing failed to ﬁnd the ground states for these hardest instances.

figures.shows: Density scatter of DW gauge averaged (y) against simulated classical annealer SA (x) success probability at 500, 1000, 5000, 10000 sweeps; wide scatter with weak diagonal structure, becoming somewhat more diagonal at 10000 sweeps.
figures.confirmed_by: The correlations are worse than for the simulated quantum annealer.

figures.shows: Heat maps of joint distribution p(s, Delta) for the simulated classical annealer at 500, 1000, 5000, 10000 sweeps (x success probability 0 to 1; y energy difference 0 to 20; log colour scale 10^-6 to 10^0). Weight moves toward higher s and lower Delta with more sweeps.
figures.confirmed_by: Shown is the joint probability distribution p(s, ∆) (colour scale) of success probability s and the ﬁnal state energy ∆ measured relative to the ground state.

figures.shows: Time to solution of exact solvers (y, 10^-3 to 10^4 s) against sqrt(N) (8 to 512): belief propagation 16 cores and divide and conquer 16 cores rise from about 4x10^-3 s to about 100 s at N = 512; Spinglass server and Akmaxsat rise much faster and stop at about N = 200.
figures.confirmed_by: Figure 24 shows the time scaling of the exact solvers for instances without ﬁelds.

figures.shows: Time to solution (y, 10^-3 to 10^4 s) against sqrt(N) up to N = 200, for instances without fields, with percentile curves: A) spin glass server (99% curve to about 10^3 s at N = 200), B) akmaxsat (rising much faster, to over 10^3 s).
figures.confirmed_by: The scaling for the various percentiles from the easiest (1% percentile) to the hardest (99% percentile) is shown in ﬁgures 25 and 26 for instances with and without local ﬁelds.

figures.shows: Same as Supplementary Figure 25 for instances with fields: A) spin glass server with fields (99% to about 300 s at N = 200), B) akmaxsat with fields (99% to about 2000 s).
figures.confirmed_by: The scaling for the various percentiles from the easiest (1% percentile) to the hardest (99% percentile) is shown in ﬁgures 25 and 26 for instances with and without local ﬁelds.

figures.shows: Median (50% quantile) total effort of simulated annealing in sweeps (y, 10^1 to 10^9) against sqrt(N) (8 to 512) for fixed sweep counts 5 to 10000 and the optimal. Fixed-time curves rise modestly then shoot upward when the time becomes too short; the optimal curve rises smoothly (exponentially in sqrt N).
figures.confirmed_by: This graph demonstrates that extrapolating results for ﬁxed annealing times does not give the true asymptotic behaviour.

figures.shows: Total effort against annealing time for N = 108, no fields, percentile curves. A) SA: total spin flips against sweeps (10^1 to 10^5): U-shaped with minimum near about 100 sweeps. B) SQA: U-shaped with minimum near about 100 sweeps. C) DW: total time (microseconds) against annealing time (1 to 10^4 microseconds): monotonically increasing, no minimum.
figures.confirmed_by: Note that a minimum is not found for the D-Wave device but instead a monotonic increase, indicating that even the fastest annealing time of the hardware of tf = 5µs is slower than the optimal time.

figures.shows: Scaling with fields against sqrt(N) (8 to 512). A) DW gauge averaged with fields: total time (10^-7 to 10^0 s), medians near about 5 microseconds. B) SA with fields: spin flips (10^2 to 10^9). C) SQA with fields: spin updates times beta (10^4 to 10^11); arrows for 1 ms and 1 s reference machines.
figures.confirmed_by: Scaling plot with ﬁelds for A) QA, B) SA and C) SQA.

figures.shows: Total effort per spin (divided by N) for instances without fields against sqrt(N) (8 to 512) with percentile curves. A) SA: sweeps, from about 20 to about 10^8 (99%). B) SQA: spin updates times beta over N, from about 100 to about 10^9; the 99% and 95% curves stop at N of about 288 and 392.
figures.confirmed_by: Scaling of total annealing eﬀort assuming parallel updates of spins for instances without ﬁelds.

figures.shows: As Supplementary Figure 30 with local fields: A) SA with fields, sweeps (10^1 to 10^8); B) SQA with fields (10^2 to 10^9), against sqrt(N) from 8 to 512.
figures.confirmed_by: As in ﬁgure 30 the total eﬀort is divided by the system size due to the intrinsic parallelism of an experimental quantum annealer.

figures.shows: Correlation function C(tau) (log y, 0.001 to 1) against imaginary time tau (0 to 10), red points with a blue exponential fit line over the large-tau region; C falls from about 0.7 at tau = 0 to about 0.002 at tau = 10.
figures.confirmed_by: The line shows an exponential ﬁt. The gap can be obtained from the slope of the line.

figures.shows: Ten panels of the lowest excitation gap Delta (y, in units of B(t), 0 to about 2.5) against Gamma (x, 0 to 3), blue points with error bars and a red temperature line. Left column five easy instances, right column five hard instances. The gap closes near Gamma of about 2.2 to 2.5 and toward Gamma = 0; hard instances show additional small gaps at lower Gamma.
figures.confirmed_by: Shown is the lowest excitation gap for the two instances presented in the main text, along with eight additional, complementary instances.

figures.shows: Performance of the classical annealer on the reference hardware: Intel Xeon E5-2670 1 core 5 spin flips per ns (relative speed 1); 8 cores 40 (8); Nvidia Tesla K20X GPU 210 (42).
figures.confirmed_by: The performance of our codes on the classical reference hardware is shown in Table I.

figures.shows: Performance of simulated quantum annealers in spin updates per microsecond (relative speed): CTQ 1 core 1.3 (1); CTQ 8 cores 3.8 (8); DTQ 1 core 5.8 (4.5); DTQ 8 cores 46 (35), on an Intel Xeon E5-2670 CPU, schedule II, inverse temperature 10.
figures.confirmed_by: We show performance ﬁgures of both our continuous time (CTQ) and discrete time (DTQ) implementations on an Intel Xeon E5-2670 CPU using schedule II at inverse temperature β = 10.

papers.what_it_is: Boixo, Rønnow, Isakov, Wang, Wecker, Lidar, Martinis and Troyer test a 108-qubit D-Wave One device against simulated annealing, simulated quantum annealing and classical spin dynamics on random Ising spin glass instances, to ask whether it performs quantum annealing and how its effort scales.

assertions.value: The authors state that of the 128 qubits on the D-Wave One device, 108 were fully functioning and were used in their experiments.
quotes: Of the 128 qubits on the device, 108 were fully functioning and were used in our experiments.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own experimental setup in the Experimental results section.

assertions.value: The authors randomly assigned each coupler Jij in the device a value of either +1 or −1, which they say gives a very rough energy landscape.
quotes: For each coupler Jij in the device we randomly assigned a value of either +1 or −1, giving rise to a very rough energy landscape.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states how its test problems were generated, in the Experimental results section.

assertions.value: The authors set all local fields hi to 0 for most of the data shown in the main text and give data with local fields in the supplementary material.
quotes: We thus set all hi = 0 for most data shown here and provide data with local ﬁelds in the supplementary material.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the scope of its main-text data in the Experimental results section.

assertions.value: The authors ran problems of sizes from N = 8 to N = 108, with 1000 different instances per size and M = 1000 annealing runs per instance, and determined whether each run reached the ground state.
quotes: We performed experiments for problems of sizes ranging from N = 8 to N = 108.
we selected 1000 diﬀerent instances by choosing 1000 sets of diﬀerent random couplings Jij = ±1
For each of these instances, we performed M = 1000 annealing runs and determined whether the system reached the ground state.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own experimental design in the Experimental results section.

assertions.value: The Methods state that after programming the couplings the device was cooled for 2.5 s, and then 1000 annealing runs were performed with an annealing time of tf = 5 µs.
quotes: the device was cooled for 2.5 s
then 1000 annealing runs were performed using an annealing time of tf = 5 µs.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own run protocol in the Methods section.

assertions.value: The Methods state that annealing is performed at a temperature of 0.4 GHz, with the transverse field starting at about 5 GHz and going to zero, and the couplings and local fields reaching about 5 GHz at the end of the schedule.
quotes: Annealing is performed at a temperature of 0.4 GHz
A(0) ≈ 5 GHz, going to zero during the annealing
about B(tf ) ≈ 5 GHz at the end of the schedule.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the device schedule it ran, in the Methods section.

assertions.value: The authors state that the device temperature is 20mK (0.4 GHz).
quotes: than the device temperature of 20mK (0.4 GHz)
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the device temperature as part of its setup.
assertions.reader_inference: Supplementary VII (p.22) gives the physical temperature as 17 mK, which differs from this 20mK.

assertions.value: The authors state that the physical temperature is constant at 17 mK.
quotes: While the physical temperature is constant (17 mK)
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the physical temperature as part of its setup.
assertions.reader_inference: Supplementary III.B (p.9) gives the device temperature as 20mK (0.4 GHz); the two numbers differ within the same paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that finding the ground state of the Ising spin glass is NP hard, meaning it is at least as hard as the hardest problems in NP, citing earlier work.
quotes: This problem is nondeterministic polynomially (NP) hard [14], meaning that it is at least as hard as the hardest problems in NP
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors report that the D-Wave device, the simulated quantum annealer and the classical spin dynamics model all show a bimodal distribution of success probabilities, with a clear split into easy and hard instances.
quotes: In contrast, the D-Wave device, the simulated quantum annealer and the spin dynamics model exhibit a bimodal distribution, with a clear split into easy and hard instances.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors report that the success probability distribution of the D-Wave results matches well with simulated quantum annealing, moderately with spin dynamics, and poorly with simulated classical annealing.
quotes: where we see that the DW results match well with SQA, moderately with SD, and poorly with SA.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors report a unimodal success probability distribution for the simulated classical annealer for all schedules, temperatures and annealing times they tried, with a peak position that moves to the right as the annealing time tf increases.
quotes: We ﬁnd a unimodal distribution for the simulated annealer model for all schedules, temperatures and annealing times we tried, with a peak position that moves to the right as one increases tf
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors report very similar joint distributions of success probability and final-state energy for the D-Wave device (panel A) and the simulated quantum annealer (panel B).
quotes: We ﬁnd very similar results for the D-Wave device (panel A) and the simulated quantum annealer (panel B).
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors report that the joint distribution for simulated classical annealing (panel C) matches that of the D-Wave device poorly, and that for spin dynamics (panel D) matches only moderately.
quotes: The distribution for simulated classical annealing (panel C) matches poorly and for spin dynamics (panel D) matches only moderately.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors report that the density in the lower left corner (hard for both methods) and the upper right corner (easy for both methods) of the scatter plot of success probabilities confirms similarities between the D-Wave device and a simulated quantum annealer, and that the similarity to the device-to-device baseline suggests almost perfect correlation with SQA to within calibration uncertainties.
quotes: The high density in the lower left corner (hard for both methods) and the upper right corner (easy for both methods) conﬁrms the similarities between the D-Wave device and a simulated quantum annealer.
The similarity to panel A) suggests almost perfect correlation with SQA, to within calibration uncertainties.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors report no apparent correlation between the hard instances for the spin dynamics model and the success probability on the device.
quotes: there is no apparent correlation between the hard instances for the spin dynamics model and the success probability on the device
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors state that the correlations between the simulated classical annealer and the D-Wave device are significantly worse than between SQA and the device.
quotes: The correlations between the simulated classical annealer and the D-Wave device, shown in the supplementary material, are signiﬁcantly worse than between SQA and the device.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors state that when the temperature is lowered in the simulated quantum annealer, thermal updates are suppressed, quantum tunneling dominates thermal barrier crossing, and they observe a stronger bimodality.
quotes: When lowering the temperature thermal updates are suppressed, quantum tunneling dominates thermal barrier crossing, and we observe a stronger bimodality
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors state that thermal effects become more important as the temperature is increased, and eventually the bimodality vanishes.
quotes: In contrast, thermal eﬀects become more important as we increase the temperature, and eventually the bimodality vanishes
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors report that for all instances studied by quantum Monte Carlo, the gap trivially closes around a ratio Γ = A(t)/B(t) of about 2.3 of transverse field to Ising coupling, related to a global Z2 spin inversion symmetry.
quotes: For all instances, we found that the gap trivially closes around a ratio Γ = A(t)/B(t) ≈ 2.3 of transverse ﬁeld to Ising coupling, related to a global Z2 spin inversion symmetry.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from quantum Monte Carlo simulation of ten instances in one study.
assertions.reader_inference: Supplementary VII (p.22) says the gap closes trivially around Γ = 2.2.

assertions.value: The authors report that the hard instances typically have additional avoided level crossings with small gaps, seen at Γ ≈ 0.5 in the right panel of Figure 4.
quotes: The hard instances, however, typically have additional avoided level crossings with small gaps as is seen at Γ ≈ 0.5 in the right panel of ﬁgure 4.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors state that these additional avoided level crossings cause failures of the annealing due to transitions to higher energy states, thus making the problem hard.
quotes: These additional avoided level crossings cause failures of the annealing due to transitions to higher energy states, thus making the problem “hard”.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's explanation supported by gap calculations on a few instances, not proved.

assertions.value: The authors report that for the easy instances the Hamming distance of excited states found by the device is typically small, and that the hard instances typically result in excited states with a large Hamming distance.
quotes: We ﬁnd that for the “easy” instances the Hamming distance is typically small.
The “hard” instances on the other hand typically result in excited states with a large Hamming distance.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors state that, combining their observations, they have strong evidence for quantum behaviour in the device.
quotes: Combining all these observations we have strong evidence for quantum behaviour in the device
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's conclusion from empirical comparisons in one study.

assertions.value: The authors conclude that their experiments have demonstrated that quantum annealing with more than one hundred qubits takes place in the D-Wave One device, despite limited qubit coherence times.
quotes: Our experiments have demonstrated that quantum annealing with more than one hundred qubits takes place in the D-Wave One device, despite limited qubit coherence times.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's conclusion from empirical comparisons in one study.

assertions.value: The authors state that sensitivity to small gaps of the quantum model demonstrates that the device has sufficient ground state quantum coherence to realise quantum annealing of a transverse field Ising model.
quotes: Sensitivity to these small gaps of the quantum model demonstrates that the device has suﬃcient ground state quantum coherence to realise quantum annealing of a transverse ﬁeld Ising model.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's conclusion from empirical comparisons in one study.

assertions.value: The authors report that an exact version of belief propagation performed fastest of four exact algorithms, requiring around 60 ms for N = 128 and 3 minutes for N = 512 on 16 cores of an Intel Xeon CPU.

assertions.certainty_reason: An author's methodological recommendation without a proof.

assertions.value: The authors state that, assuming the minimum programmable annealing time on future D-Wave devices does not increase too rapidly, they expect that perhaps already for a device with N = 512 spins, or possibly N = 2048 spins, the optimal annealing time tf for a single run will be within reach.
quotes: we expect that perhaps already for a device with N = 512 spins, or possibly N = 2048 spins, the optimal annealing time tf for a single run will be within reach.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's expectation, stated as conditional and not tested.

assertions.value: The authors state that for the gap calculation they anneal the system from Γ = 3 to small Γ in steps of 0.1 using the continuous time algorithm, with simulations at inverse temperatures β = 100 and β = 200.
quotes: “anneal” the system from Γ = 3 to small values of Γ in steps of 0.1.
Simulations are done at inverse temperatures β = 100 and β = 200.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own gap calculation setup.

assertions.value: The authors state that, generally, all gaps shown in their gap figures are upper bounds for the gap to the lowest excited state.

assertions.value: The authors state in the supplement that the gap closes trivially around Γ = 2.2, related to a global Z2 symmetry breaking.

assertions.value: The authors state that the last easy instance shown in Figure 33 does have a small gap, which shows that a small gap is not a sufficient condition for making a problem hard.
quotes: This shows that a small gap is not a suﬃcient condition for making a problem “hard”.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical observation from one instance.
